title: the sound the universe hums
hook: the sound a room makes together; it's three sounds and a silence
tomorrow: the thing that's yours to do

segments.voice: Yesterday: namaste. Namas, a bow; te, to you. Today, the sound that opens almost every Hindu prayer.

Om. A yoga class ends with it, and a lot of Hindu prayers begin with it. Most people treat it as one long hum. One of the Upanishads hears four parts in it: three sounds, and a fourth that isn't a sound at all. First, a guess.

Say it slowly and you can feel three sounds. A, with the mouth open. U, as the lips round. M, as they close. That's why it's sometimes written aum. The Mandukya Upanishad, a text of just twelve verses, starts by saying om is all of this: past, present, future, and whatever lies beyond time. Then it maps the sounds onto your day. A is waking, the world you can see and touch. U is dreaming, the world made of the mind. M is deep, dreamless sleep, where nothing is wanted. The fourth part has no sound. It's the silence after the m runs out, and the text calls it simply the fourth: the self, at peace. So om isn't a sign-off. It's a map of a whole day in one breath, with the quiet underneath it. The Bhagavad Gita says acts of offering, giving and discipline begin with it.
screen: `A — WAKING.` · `U — DREAMING.` · `M — DEEP SLEEP.` · `THE FOURTH — THE SILENCE.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Breathe in. Let it out as the sound, aloud or under your breath: a, u, m. Let the m run out on its own, then stay a second in the quiet after it. That quiet is the fourth part.
Om. A, u and m for waking, dreaming and deep sleep, and the silence after it for the fourth. Second word on your strand.

howItsDone: Hindus chant om at the start of prayers, mantras and readings of scripture, often at the end too, and it is written as a single sacred sign, ॐ, in homes and temples.

story.title: the boy who waited for Death
story.text: In the Katha Upanishad, a boy named Nachiketa is sent, in his angry father's words, to Death. He goes. Yama, the lord of death, is away, and the boy waits three days at his door without food. To make up for it, Yama offers him three wishes. For the third, Nachiketa asks what happens after we die. Yama offers him gold, long life, kingdoms, anything else. The boy says no. So Yama teaches him, and part of the teaching is a single word: the word all the Vedas point to is om.

notes: Mandukya verse 1 (om is all this: past, present, future, and beyond the three times) and verses 8–12 (a, u, m as waking, dream, deep sleep; the soundless fourth, peaceful, the self) are paraphrased. Confirm verse numbers and that 'the self, peaceful, where the noise of the world falls away' fairly renders verse 12 (prapanchopashama, shiva, advaita).
Gita 17.24 says that for those who follow Vedic teaching, acts of sacrifice, giving and austerity begin with om; paraphrased as 'offering, giving and discipline'. Confirm.
Cut from manuscript day 2 under the claims rule: 'every yoga class on earth', 'the most-analyzed syllable in human history', the Mandukya being 'about eight hundred words' and 'one of the shortest'.
Title keeps the index ('the sound the universe hums'); the script doesn't claim the universe literally hums. Keeper may want a line on how tradition speaks of om as the primal sound.

Editor pass: hook no longer tells the listener they felt self-conscious ('some people feel'); 'in about ten seconds' cut to 'in a single breath' under the claims rule; Mandukya ref widened to 1, 3–5, 7–12, since the states (waking, dream, deep sleep, the fourth) are described in 3–5 and 7 and mapped to a, u, m and the soundless fourth in 8–12.

Editor review 2: trapdoor said the Mandukya calls the fourth 'turiya'; the Mandukya's own word is chaturtha (verses 7, 12), and turiya is the later term (Gaudapada and others), so the floor now says both. Spoken lines read and left as they were.
